intervention.description: 3D ink-extrusion printing followed by de-binding under H2 and sintering under vacuum

structure.description: nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy

evidence_units.mechanism: Sequential decomposition of hydride powders followed by sintering at 1400 °C
evidence_spans: Additive manufacturing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is implemented by extruding inks containing hydride powders, de‐binding under H 2 , and sintering under vacuum.
The sequential decomposition of hydride powders (HfH 2 +NbH+TaH 0.5 +TiH 2 +ZrH 2 ) is followed by in situ X‐ray diffraction.
Upon sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, a nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy is synthesized; on slow cooling, both α‐HCP and β‐BCC phases are formed

intervention.description: Rapid cooling from sintering temperature

evidence_units.mechanism: Quenching prevents phase separation observed during slow cooling
evidence_spans: but on quenching, a metastable single β‐BCC phase is obtained.

intervention.description: Mechanical property testing at high temperatures

evidence_units.mechanism: Presence of ≈1 wt.% O in printed and sintered HfNbTaTiZr alloys
evidence_spans: Printed and sintered HfNbTaTiZr alloys with ≈1 wt.% O shows excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures.

intervention.description: Pack cementation with silicide

evidence_units.mechanism: Silicide coating provides a barrier against oxidation
evidence_spans: Oxidation resistance is achieved by silicide coating via pack cementation.

material.name: microlattice core sandwich

intervention.description: Exposure to high‐temperature flames

evidence_units.mechanism: Sequential approach (printing, sintering, and siliconizing) enables high‐temperature performance
evidence_spans: A small‐size lattice‐core sandwich is fabricated and tested with high‐temperature flames to demonstrate the versatility of this sequential approach (printing, sintering, and siliconizing) for high‐temperature, high‐stress applications of refractory high‐entropy alloys.

material.name: HfNbTaTiZr RHEA ink
material.composition: Metallic/hydride powders (TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5) with polystyrene binder

intervention.description: Layer-by-layer extrusion of filaments

structure.description: Loosely packed powder blend consisting of TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, and TaH0.5

evidence_units.mechanism: Solvent (dichloromethane, DCM) evaporation near-instantaneously and binder (polystyrene, PS) precipitation leading to a quick increase in the strength of filaments
evidence_spans: The ≈410 µm filaments containing metallic/hydride powders are printed layer by layer to produce complex parts, including a lattice sandwich structure, as shown in Figure 1b . When the filaments are extruded, the solvent (dichloromethane, DCM) evaporates near‐instantaneously, and the binder (polystyrene, PS) precipitates, leading to a quick increase in the strength of filaments that helps the structure to self‐support.

intervention.description: Uniaxial compressive stress-strain testing

structure.description: Multiphase (β‐BCC1 + β‐BCC2 + α‐HCP) microstructure with coarse grains (≈28 ± 14 µm) and interstitial O and C

evidence_units.mechanism: Interstitial solid-solution strengthening from oxygen and carbon, and dynamic recovery and recrystallization
evidence_spans: Figure 4a,b shows that the yield strength is much higher for sintered HfNbTaTiZr bulk than for arc‐melted HfNbTaTiZr reported in Refs. [ [25] , [45] ] between 750 to 1100 °C.

intervention.description: Subjecting to acetylene flame

evidence_units.mechanism: Low thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr combined with complex porous architecture improves thermal insulation
evidence_spans: After 120 s heating, the highest local temperature on the hot side is 1100 °C with an average temperature of ≈520 °C, while the average temperature on the cold side is ≈270 °C (Figure 1d ). This demonstrates our method's robustness and flexibility for rapid prototyping of RHEA for high‐temperature, ductile, low‐mass insulating structures.

intervention.description: Silicide coating via fluoride activator and Si source

structure.description: Two distinct silicide layers with cracks
phases: MSi2 (M = Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)
MSi (M = Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)
defects: Cracks ending at the interface between silicide and substrate

evidence_units.mechanism: Inward diffusion of Si driven by chemical potential gradient
evidence_spans: During pack cementation at 950 °C for 24 h, the fluoride activator reacts with the Si source to form gaseous SiF 4 , which deposits Si on the sample driven by the chemical potential gradient in the pack. Because Si is the faster diffusing element in the silicide of Ti, [ [54] ] Zr, [ [55] ] Hf, [ [55] ] Nb, [ [56] ] and Ta, [ [57] ] inward diffusion of Si occurs from the surface of the sample, thus forming two distinct silicide layers as shown in Figure 5 a . The first layer, with a thickness of 40 ± 2 µm, has a high silicon content (69 at.%) which roughly corresponds to MSi 2 (M = Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, and Ta).

intervention.description: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) under airflow

evidence_units.mechanism: Formation of (Zr,Hf)O2 filling cracks and growth of silicide layer underneath prevents run-away oxidation
evidence_spans: In Figure 5b , for the first 1–3 h of oxidation, the specimens appear to follow the parabolic law, and parabolic rate constants can be determined for the uncoated sample ( k = 570 mg 2 cm −4 h −1 ), which is ≈700 times higher than that of silicide‐coated sample ( k = 0.80 mg 2 cm −4 h −1 ), indicating much higher oxidation resistance for the silicide‐coated samples.

intervention.description: TGA and microscopy after prolonged exposure

structure.description: Silicide layer with pre-existing cracks filled with (Zr,Hf)O2 and deeper incursion of silicide

evidence_units.mechanism: Self-healing mechanism: Zr and Hf react with oxygen to form oxide, expelling Si deeper
evidence_spans: After 10 h oxidation, the uncoated sample has a Δ m / A of 148 mg cm −2 , which is ≈30 times higher than 5.2 mg cm −2 for the silicide‐coated sample. This shows that the silicide layer is still quite protective, well beyond the early parabolic oxidation stage.

material.form: Powder blend (Ti, ZrH2, HfH2, Nb, TaH0.5) printed into lattices and bulk ingots
material.initial_state: Green body after 3D printing and drying

intervention.description: Evaporation of residual DCM/EGBE followed by decomposition of PS binder polymer

structure.description: De-bound green body prior to sintering

evidence_units.mechanism: Removal of organic solvents and polymer binder to prepare for sintering
evidence_spans: First, the printed samples were exposed to flowing hydrogen (99.999% pure) for de‐binding. Two steps were included in the de‐binding stage: i) evaporation of residual DCM solvent and EGBE at 150 °C for 30 min, and ii) decomposition of the PS binder polymer at 450 °C for 30 min. The heating and cooling rates are 10 °C min −1 .

material.name: HfNbTaTiZr alloy
material.composition: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (with Ti and Nb over-stoichiometric)
material.form: 3D printed lattices (9 × 9 × 9 mm 3) and bulk ingots

intervention.description: Vacuum sintering to densify the printed parts

evidence_units.mechanism: Solid-state sintering promoted by oxygen gettering to achieve densification

outcome.measurement_method: Measured via linear shrinkage and optical micrographs

evidence_spans: Second, sintering was performed at 1400 °C, for times spanning between 15 min and 18 h, in a vacuum tube furnace with an initial vacuum level of < 3 × 10 −6 torr. A zirconium foil was used to cover the crucible containing the samples and titanium sponges were placed in the crucible to act as an oxygen getter during sintering.

intervention.description: High-temperature heat treatment followed by water quenching to study phase transformations

evidence_units.mechanism: Homogenization of alloying elements followed by rapid cooling to retain high-temperature phases

outcome.measurement_method: Not explicitly quantified in text, studied via characterization

evidence_spans: Some sintered samples were then wrapped with Mo foil, sealed in an evacuated quartz tube, heated at 1500 °C for 1 h for homogenization, and then water quenched, to study phase transformations in the alloy.

intervention.description: Compression tests to measure yield strength at elevated temperatures

parameters.intermediate_steps: Load removed after ≈0.2% plastic strain, temperature increased by ≈100 °C

evidence_units.mechanism: Plastic deformation under compressive load at elevated temperatures

outcome.unit: MPa (implied by context, but not stated)

evidence_spans: High‐temperature compression tests were carried out at an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −4 s −1 on an MTS‐5 servo‐hydraulic tester with a furnace using flowing argon (99.999% pure). To ensure uniaxial compression, the top and bottom surfaces of sintered samples were ground flat and parallel before the compression test. Then, the sintered lattices (≈5.6 × 5.6 × 5.6 mm 3 ) and bulk cylindrical samples (D:5.7 mm, H:11.7 mm) were placed between boron‐nitride‐coated platens and wrapped with Ti foils as oxygen getter. Yield strengths of two bulk cylindrical samples were measured between 800 and 1100 °C and between 750 and 1050 °C, respectively. After yielding (plastic strain: ≈0.2%), the load was removed, and the temperature was increased by ≈100 °C to the next temperature. The subsequent load‐yield‐unload measurement took place after the temperature was stabilized, and this procedure was repeated until the highest temperature was reached.

intervention.description: Measurement of mass gain during oxidation

structure.description: Uncoated and silicide-coated specimens during oxidation

evidence_spans: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was carried out on Mettler Toledo TGA/DSC 3+ instrument. The sintered specimens – uncoated (74 mg, cuboid, 1.8 × 2.2 × 2.1 mm) and silicide‐coated (112 mg, near half disk, R: 3.0 mm, H: 0.9 mm, surface area calculated from optical images) – were placed in alumina crucibles and mass gain was measured at 1000 °C for 20 h under dry air (50 mL min −1 flow rate).

intervention.description: Laser-flash analysis to measure thermal diffusivity and calculate thermal conductivity

evidence_units.mechanism: Laser-flash analysis to determine thermal diffusivity, converted to thermal conductivity using density and Dulong–Petit law
evidence_spans: Thermal diffusivity ( D T ) of the sintered samples between 50 and 900 °C was measured by Laser‐flash analysis (Netzsch LFA 457, Germany). The thermal conductivity was calculated according to k = ρ c p D T , where ρ is the density (9.72 g cm −3[ [69] ] ), and c p is the specific heat capacity (approximated by the Dulong–Petit law).

intervention.action: Dehydrogenation study via in situ XRD
intervention.description: Temperature-dependent dehydrogenation under vacuum

evidence_units.mechanism: Dehydrogenation of metal hydrides leading to phase transformation
evidence_spans: In situ X‐ray diffraction was performed on a STADI MP instrument to study the dehydrogenation mechanisms. The measurement was performed with a Mo source on the TiH 2 ‐ZrH 2 ‐HfH 2 ‐NbH‐TaH 0.5 powder blend (target composition: equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr) lodged in an externally heated quartz capillary (0.3 mm ID). The hydride powder blend was obtained after hydrogenating extruded ink at 730 °C for 2 h under pure hydrogen. The subsequent dehydrogenation experiments were performed under vacuum (≈10 −3 torr) while increasing temperature from 100 to 1000 °C with diffraction spectra collected at each 5 °C step with 18.54° 2θ angular coverage and 120 s exposure.
